Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Models for Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features
papers.research_question: How can neural network models for toxicity prediction be interpreted by extracting learned chemical features from hidden layers?
papers.core_contribution: A novel method to interpret neural network predictions for toxicity by extracting chemical substructures from hidden neurons, validated on mutagenicity data and shown to be competitive with established attribution methods.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a novel method to extract learned chemical information from hidden layers of neural networks and use these to explain model predictions, complementing more established techniques for understanding neural network models for toxicity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The activation of hidden neurons in a neural network trained for toxicity prediction can be linked to specific chemical substructures (toxicophores).
The proposed method can extract substructures that correspond to known toxicophores for mutagenicity.
The explanations provided by the method (IG_hidden) are competitive with and complementary to those from input feature attribution (IG_input).
The method works well for single-layer networks but for deeper layers, neurons tend to aggregate multiple features and become less specific.
papers.limitation:
One neuron may be activated by a range of diverse chemical substructures, making it impossible to assign a single cause to the activation of a particular neuron.
Relevant chemical features may activate a large number of different neurons across the network, making interpretation complex.
It could be that none of the identified substructures associated with a highly activated neuron match the test compound.
future_direction: Extending the approach to regression models.
Using more generic representations of substructures such as SMARTS.
Applying the method to other toxicity endpoints and datasets.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have become a popular machine-learning technique for the toxicity prediction of chemicals. However, due to their complex structure, it is difficult to understand predictions made by these models which limits confidence. Current techniques to tackle this problem such as SHAP or integrated gradients provide insights by attributing importance to the input features of individual compounds. While these methods have produced promising results in some cases, they do not shed light on how representations of compounds are transformed in hidden layers, which constitute how neural networks learn. We present a novel technique to interpret neural networks which identifies chemical substructures in training data found to be responsible for the activation of hidden neurons. For individual test compounds, the importance of hidden neurons is determined, and the associated substructures are leveraged to explain the model prediction. Using structural alerts for mutagenicity from the Derek Nexus expert system as ground truth, we demonstrate the validity of the approach and show that model explanations are competitive with and complementary to explanations obtained from an established feature attribution method.

papers.title: Harmonics of Learning: Universal Fourier Features Emerge in Invariant Networks
papers.research_question: Why do Fourier features universally emerge in neural networks and other learning systems that are invariant to group symmetries?
papers.core_contribution: This work formally proves that if a parametric function (e.g., a neural network) is invariant to a finite group, then its weights recover the Fourier transform on that group, providing a mathematical explanation for the emergence of universal Fourier features.
papers.conclusion: Invariance to group symmetries forces neural networks to learn Fourier features, providing a foundational algebraic theory for universal representations in biological and artificial learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Invariant parametric functions have weights that coincide with irreducible unitary group representations (harmonics) up to linear transformation.
If the weights are orthonormal, they coincide with the Fourier transform of the group.
The multiplication table of an unknown group can be recovered from the weights of an approximately invariant model.
Spectral Networks, McCulloch-Pitts neurons, and deep networks (first layer) satisfy the conditions for unitary symmetries and thus exhibit this behavior.
papers.limitation: The current theory assumes free group actions on the input data; extending it to non-free actions (with stabilizers) requires further clarification and is beyond the scope of this work.
future_direction: Extending the theory to group actions that are not free, which requires handling stabilizers.
papers.abstract: In this work, we formally prove that, under certain conditions, if a neural network is invariant to a finite group then its weights recover the Fourier transform on that group. This provides a mathematical explanation for the emergence of Fourier features -- a ubiquitous phenomenon in both biological and artificial learning systems. The results hold even for non-commutative groups, in which case the Fourier transform encodes all the irreducible unitary group representations. Our findings have consequences for the problem of symmetry discovery. Specifically, we demonstrate that the algebraic structure of an unknown group can be recovered from the weights of a network that is at least approximately invariant within certain bounds. Overall, this work contributes to a foundation for an algebraic learning theory of invariant neural network representations.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Emergence of Quantised Representations Isolated to Anisotropic Functions
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of activation functions (discrete vs. continuous) influence the emergence and organization of discrete representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that activation functions defined by discrete algebraic symmetries (e.g., permutation-equivariance) induce a quantizing inductive bias, leading to discrete, symmetry-organized clusters in representations, whereas functions with continuous symmetries (e.g., orthogonal-equivariance) preserve more continuous representations.
papers.conclusion: The symmetry properties of activation functions act as a strong inductive bias, with discrete symmetries leading to quantized representations and continuous symmetries preserving continuity, implying that many observed interpretability structures are not fundamental but arise from specific architectural choices.
papers.key_findings:
Discrete symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., standard tanh) cause representations to cluster around distinguished directions, leading to quantized, discrete structures.
Continuous symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., isotropic tanh) do not induce such task-agnostic clustering, resulting in more continuous representations.
The observed quantisation effect correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, suggesting potential pathological consequences.
The Privileged-Plane Projective Method (PPP) is introduced as a tool for high-fidelity visualization of representational geometry, preserving both angular and magnitude information.
The findings suggest that many interpretability phenomena (e.g., grandmother neurons, discrete coding) may be contingent on the choice of anisotropic functional forms rather than fundamental to deep learning.
papers.limitation:
The performance analysis (reconstruction error) is preliminary, as the isotropic activation functions are placeholder designs not optimized for performance.
The study is conducted on relatively small autoencoder models; the findings may not generalize directly to larger, more complex architectures like transformers.
future_direction: Further investigation into the pathological implications of function-driven quantisation, such as effects on adversarial robustness and representational capacity.
Exploration of isotropic functional forms in larger model architectures and their potential performance benefits.
Development of a more comprehensive taxonomy of symmetry-defined functional forms and their representational biases.
papers.abstract: Presented is a novel methodology for determining representational structure, which builds upon the existing Spotlight Resonance method. This new tool is used to gain insight into how discrete representations can emerge and organise in autoencoder models, through a controlled ablation study that alters only the activation function. Using this technique, the validity of whether function-driven symmetries can act as implicit inductive biases on representations is determined. Representations are found to tend to discretise when the activation functions are defined through a discrete algebraic permutation-equivariant symmetry. In contrast, they remain continuous under a continuous algebraic orthogonal-equivariant definition. This confirms the hypothesis that the symmetries of network primitives can carry unintended inductive biases, leading to task-independent artefactual structures in representations. The discrete symmetry of contemporary forms is shown to be a strong predictor for the production of symmetry-organised discrete representations emerging from otherwise continuous distributions -- a quantisation effect. This motivates further reassessment of functional forms in common usage due to such unintended consequences. Moreover, this supports a general causal model for a mode in which discrete representations may form, and could constitute a prerequisite for downstream interpretability phenomena, including grandmother neurons, discrete coding schemes, general linear features and a type of Superposition. Hence, this tool and proposed mechanism for the influence of functional form on representations may provide insights into interpretability research. Finally, preliminary results indicate that quantisation of representations correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, reinforcing previous conjectures that this collapse can be detrimental.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: nDNA -- the Semantic Helix of Artificial Cognition
papers.research_question: How can we characterize and compare the latent semantic genomes of diverse LLMs? What geometric invariants define model ancestry, inheritance, and epistemic divergence?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures the latent identity of foundation models through the intrinsic geometry of belief, integrating spectral curvature, thermodynamic length, and belief gradients to form a diagnostic framework for neural genomics.
papers.conclusion: Proposes nDNA and Neural Genomics as a framework for understanding the evolving anatomy of artificial cognition, offering a grammar for diagnosing and governing model lineage, drift, and internal alignment.
papers.abstract: As AI foundation models grow in capability, a deeper question emerges: What shapes their internal cognitive identity -- beyond fluency and output? Benchmarks measure behavior, but the soul of a model resides in its latent geometry. In this work, we propose Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures this latent identity through the intrinsic geometry of belief. At its core, nDNA is synthesized from three principled and indispensable dimensions of latent geometry: spectral curvature, which reveals the curvature of conceptual flow across layers; thermodynamic length, which quantifies the semantic effort required to traverse representational transitions through layers; and belief vector field, which delineates the semantic torsion fields that guide a model's belief directional orientations. Like biological DNA, it encodes ancestry, mutation, and semantic inheritance, found in finetuning and alignment scars, cultural imprints, and architectural drift. In naming it, we open a new field: Neural Genomics, where models are not just tools, but digital semantic organisms with traceable inner cognition. Modeling statement. We read AI foundation models as semantic fluid dynamics: meaning is transported through layers like fluid in a shaped conduit; nDNA is the physics-grade readout of that flow -- a geometry-first measure of how meaning is bent, paid for, and pushed -- yielding a stable, coordinate-free neural DNA fingerprint tied to on-input behavior; with this fingerprint we cross into biology: tracing lineages across pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment, pruning, distillation, and merges; measuring inheritance between checkpoints; detecting drift as traits shift under new data or objectives; and, ultimately, studying the evolution of artificial cognition to compare models, diagnose risks, and govern change over time.

papers.title: SALSA: Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we learn semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, using SMILES-based autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SALSA, a transformer-autoencoder with a contrastive loss, to learn molecular representations that capture graph-to-graph similarities, resulting in a semantically organized latent space.
papers.conclusion: SALSA learns semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, with improved interpolation and property awareness, and can be applied to other domains with user-defined semantics.
papers.key_findings:
SALSA achieves higher correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance in latent space compared to a naive autoencoder.
SALSA generates more semantically reasonable interpolations between molecules, indicating better semantic continuity.
SALSA implicitly encodes physicochemical properties better than baselines, showing improved property awareness.
The contrastive loss improves structural awareness, while the reconstruction loss acts as a regularizer to prevent degenerative mappings.
SALSA's performance degrades only at very low latent dimensions (e.g., 2 or 4), suggesting robustness down to 8 dimensions.
papers.limitation: The correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance may not hold for molecules that are substantially different
papers.abstract: In deep learning for drug discovery, chemical data are often represented as simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) sequences which allow for straightforward implementation of natural language processing methodologies, one being the sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. However, we observe that training an autoencoder solely on SMILES is insufficient to learn molecular representations that are semantically meaningful, where semantics are defined by the structural (graph-to-graph) similarities between molecules. We demonstrate by example that autoencoders may map structurally similar molecules to distant codes, resulting in an incoherent latent space that does not respect the structural similarities between molecules. To address this shortcoming we propose Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder (SALSA), a transformer-autoencoder modified with a contrastive task, tailored specifically to learn graph-to-graph similarity between molecules. Formally, the contrastive objective is to map structurally similar molecules (separated by a single graph edit) to nearby codes in the latent space. To accomplish this, we generate a novel dataset comprised of sets of structurally similar molecules and opt for a supervised contrastive loss that is able to incorporate full sets of positive samples. We compare SALSA to its ablated counterparts, and show empirically that the composed training objective (reconstruction and contrastive task) leads to a higher quality latent space that is more 1) structurally-aware, 2) semantically continuous, and 3) property-aware.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Learning a Fourier Transform for Linear Relative Positional Encodings in Transformers
papers.research_question: How to efficiently incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs) into linear Transformers, enabling linear complexity for both sequential and geometric data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), a class of linear Transformers that efficiently incorporate relative positional encodings (RPEs) by learning their spectral representation, achieving linear complexity and applicability to sequential and geometric data.
papers.conclusion: FLTs provide an efficient and effective method for incorporating RPEs into linear attention Transformers, with theoretical approximation guarantees and strong empirical performance across text, image, and 3D molecular data.
papers.key_findings:
FLTs outperform other linear Transformers (e.g., Performer, CosFormer) on language modeling (WikiText-103) by achieving lower perplexity.
FLTs achieve higher accuracy than baselines on image classification tasks (ImageNet, Places365, Fashion-MNIST).
For 3D molecular property prediction (OC20 dataset), FLTs with RPEs provide better energy prediction accuracy (lower MAE, higher EwT) than Performers without RPEs.
FLTs maintain linear time and space complexity, being more memory-efficient than log-linear Performer baselines.
FLTs can learn local RPEs and exhibit both local and global attention patterns in language modeling.
papers.abstract: We propose a new class of linear Transformers called FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), which incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs). These include regular RPE techniques applied for sequential data, as well as novel RPEs operating on geometric data embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. FLTs construct the optimal RPE mechanism implicitly by learning its spectral representation. As opposed to other architectures combining efficient low-rank linear attention with RPEs, FLTs remain practical in terms of their memory usage and do not require additional assumptions about the structure of the RPE mask. Besides, FLTs allow for applying certain structural inductive bias techniques to specify masking strategies, e.g. they provide a way to learn the so-called local RPEs introduced in this paper and give accuracy gains as compared with several other linear Transformers for language modeling. We also thoroughly test FLTs on other data modalities and tasks, such as image classification, 3D molecular modeling, and learnable optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, for 3D molecular data, FLTs are the first Transformer architectures providing linear attention and incorporating RPE masking.

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Group Crosscoders for Mechanistic Analysis of Symmetry
papers.research_question: How do neural networks represent symmetry when it is not explicitly enforced, and how can we automatically discover and analyze these symmetrical features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces group crosscoders, a method that automates the discovery and analysis of symmetrical features in neural networks by performing dictionary learning across transformed inputs under a symmetry group, providing systematic insights into how networks represent symmetry.
papers.conclusion: Group crosscoders offer a promising new tool for mechanistic interpretability by providing systematic insights into how neural networks represent symmetry, with potential for generalization to other groups and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Group crosscoders naturally cluster features into interpretable families that correspond to previously hypothesized feature types, providing clearer separation than standard sparse autoencoders.
The transform block analysis enables automatic characterization of feature symmetries, revealing distinct patterns of invariance and equivariance for different geometric features (e.g., curves vs lines).
The method can automatically detect equivariant features and group them with their transformed counterparts.
Group crosscoders separate aspects of feature geometry that correspond to equivariance from those that do not, systemizing the notion of a feature family.
future_direction: Extending the approach to other symmetry groups (e.g., scaling or hue rotation) and other modalities.
papers.abstract: We introduce group crosscoders, an extension of crosscoders that systematically discover and analyse symmetrical features in neural networks. While neural networks often develop equivariant representations without explicit architectural constraints, understanding these emergent symmetries has traditionally relied on manual analysis. Group crosscoders automate this process by performing dictionary learning across transformed versions of inputs under a symmetry group. Applied to InceptionV1's mixed3b layer using the dihedral group $\mathrm{D}_{32}$, our method reveals several key insights: First, it naturally clusters features into interpretable families that correspond to previously hypothesised feature types, providing more precise separation than standard sparse autoencoders. Second, our transform block analysis enables the automatic characterisation of feature symmetries, revealing how different geometric features (such as curves versus lines) exhibit distinct patterns of invariance and equivariance. These results demonstrate that group crosscoders can provide systematic insights into how neural networks represent symmetry, offering a promising new tool for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Task structure and nonlinearity jointly determine learned representational geometry
papers.research_question: How do activation function, input structure, and output structure jointly determine the learned representational geometry in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The activation function (Tanh vs ReLU) has a strong impact on learned representational geometry: Tanh networks align representations with target output geometry, while ReLU networks retain more input geometry, due to differences in symmetry and asymptotic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The activation function plays a crucial role in determining whether learned representations align more with target output geometry or input geometry, shedding light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations.
papers.key_findings:
Tanh networks learn representations that reflect the structure of target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about input structure.
This difference is consistent across a broad class of parameterized tasks with varying input-output alignment.
The difference arises from asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU leading to feature neuron specialization, while Tanh's symmetry causes neurons to inherit task label structure.
When target outputs are low-dimensional, Tanh networks produce more disentangled representations than ReLU networks.
The findings generalize to multi-layer networks and convolutional networks on image classification tasks.
future_direction: Investigate the progression of target/input alignment across layers in multi-layer networks for easy vs. hard tasks.
In-depth characterization of the effect of high input noise on target alignment in ReLU networks.
papers.abstract: The utility of a learned neural representation depends on how well its geometry supports performance in downstream tasks. This geometry depends on the structure of the inputs, the structure of the target outputs, and the architecture of the network. By studying the learning dynamics of networks with one hidden layer, we discovered that the network's activation function has an unexpectedly strong impact on the representational geometry: Tanh networks tend to learn representations that reflect the structure of the target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about the structure of the raw inputs. This difference is consistently observed across a broad class of parameterized tasks in which we modulated the degree of alignment between the geometry of the task inputs and that of the task labels. We analyzed the learning dynamics in weight space and show how the differences between the networks with Tanh and ReLU nonlinearities arise from the asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU, which leads feature neurons to specialize for different regions of input space. By contrast, feature neurons in Tanh networks tend to inherit the task label structure. Consequently, when the target outputs are low dimensional, Tanh networks generate neural representations that are more disentangled than those obtained with a ReLU nonlinearity. Our findings shed light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations in neural networks.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Representation Potentials of Foundation Models for Multimodal Alignment: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes evidence for the representation potentials of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within and across modalities, and analyzes the key factors driving this potential.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes substantial evidence for the representation potential of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within individual modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to neuroscience. It analyzes the key factors that foster representation potentials and discusses open questions.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment.
Scale, architectural inductive biases, training objectives, and task and instruction diversity are key factors that foster representation potentials for alignment.
Evidence for alignment is found within vision, language, and speech modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to representations observed in neuroscience.
papers.limitation:
Differences across modalities constrain the extent to which their representations can perfectly align, as certain information may be unique to a given sensory channel.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the effectiveness and interpretability of alignment metrics, and the absence of a universally accepted standard complicates cross-study comparisons.
Training data biases and sociotechnical context shape representation spaces and constrain the universality of alignment claims.
future_direction: Pursue a deeper theoretical grounding of representation potentials.
Develop more robust evaluation frameworks for alignment.
papers.abstract: Foundation models learn highly transferable representations through large-scale pretraining on diverse data. An increasing body of research indicates that these representations exhibit a remarkable degree of similarity across architectures and modalities. In this survey, we investigate the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities. We begin by reviewing representative foundation models and the key metrics that make alignment measurable. We then synthesize empirical evidence of representation potentials from studies in vision, language, speech, multimodality, and neuroscience. The evidence suggests that foundation models often exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment. We further analyze the key factors that foster representation potentials, discuss open questions, and highlight potential challenges.

papers.title: Vision-language models learn the geometry of human perceptual space
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether vision-language models learn representations that align with human perceptual space, and whether the axes of their psychological spaces correspond to human perceptual dimensions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that vision-language models learn a representational geometry that aligns with human perceptual axes, and that this AI-derived geometry can better predict human categorization behavior than human-derived similarity spaces, acting as a denoised surrogate for human perception.
papers.conclusion: VLMs capture an idealized or denoised form of human perceptual structure, providing a scalable method for cognitive science and evidence for shared constraints on perceptual organization across different learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs produce similarity judgments that correlate well with human similarity judgments at the category level.
The psychological spaces derived from VLMs via MDS show strong alignment with human perceptual dimensions (e.g., lightness, grain size, shininess) as measured by Procrustes analysis.
VLM-derived spaces, when used as input to the Generalized Context Model (GCM), predict human classification behavior better than spaces derived from human similarity judgments.
Larger VLMs tend to yield higher correlations with human similarity judgments.
The alignment improves when using an overcomplete (10D) MDS solution for GPT-4o, suggesting that human-relevant information is distributed across additional dimensions.
papers.limitation:
Alignment of geometry is not a mechanistic explanation; LLMs/VLMs are not faithful simulators of human cognition, can be prompt- or wording-sensitive, and reflect training-distribution biases.
High geometric correspondence does not guarantee equivalence of features or computations, and shortcut solutions remain a pervasive risk.
The study is focused on a single naturalistic domain, limiting generalizability to other domains and tasks.
future_direction: Establish generalizability of findings to other domains and tasks.
Apply Explainable AI (XAI) techniques to visualize which image regions contribute to the VLM's similarity judgments to test if VLM and humans use the same evidence.
Integrate axis-level alignment with neural measurements (e.g., RSA/CKA) and active pairwise sampling to understand when and why convergence arises.
papers.abstract: In cognitive science and AI, a longstanding question is whether machines learn representations that align with those of the human mind. While current models show promise, it remains an open question whether this alignment is superficial or reflects a deeper correspondence in the underlying dimensions of representation. Here we introduce a methodology to probe the internal geometry of vision-language models (VLMs) by having them generate pairwise similarity judgments for a complex set of natural objects. Using multidimensional scaling, we recover low-dimensional psychological spaces and find that their axes show a strong correspondence with the principal axes of human perceptual space. Critically, when this AI-derived representational geometry is used as the input to a classic exemplar model of categorization, it predicts human classification behavior more accurately than a space constructed from human judgments themselves. This suggests that VLMs can capture an idealized or `denoised' form of human perceptual structure. Our work provides a scalable method to overcome a measurement bottleneck in cognitive science and demonstrates that foundation models can learn a representational geometry that is functionally relevant for modeling key aspects of human cognition, such as categorization.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Global Geometry Is Not Enough for Vision Representations
papers.research_question: Does global embedding geometry, commonly used to evaluate representation quality, predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Global embedding geometry does not predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders; functional sensitivity, measured by the Jacobian effective rank, is a strong predictor and reveals a gap arising from objective design.
papers.conclusion: Global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence; functional sensitivity is a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.
papers.key_findings:
Standard geometric metrics (e.g., isotropy, participation ratio) show near-zero correlation with compositional binding accuracy across 21 vision encoders.
Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), a measure of local input-output sensitivity, strongly correlates with binding performance.
The disparity between geometry and function arises because existing training objectives explicitly constrain global embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping largely unconstrained.
Variance-decorrelation objectives (e.g., Barlow Twins, VICReg) preserve high functional rank and achieve better binding, while other objectives (e.g., CLIP, MAE) exhibit functional rank collapse.
Alternative geometric readouts (kNN, local PCA) cannot recover binding information from frozen embeddings; linear accessibility is intrinsic to the pretraining objective.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted in a controlled synthetic setting to isolate compositional binding, and is not intended to exhaustively characterize all forms of structure in large-scale or naturalistic representations.
future_direction: Developing training objectives and evaluation benchmarks that target functional structure more directly than geometry-based criteria or linear probing.
papers.abstract: A common assumption in representation learning is that globally well-distributed embeddings support robust and generalizable representations. This focus has shaped both training objectives and evaluation protocols, implicitly treating global geometry as a proxy for representational competence. While global geometry effectively encodes which elements are present, it is often insensitive to how they are composed. We investigate this limitation by testing the ability of geometric metrics to predict compositional binding across 21 vision encoders. We find that standard geometry-based statistics exhibit near-zero correlation with compositional binding. In contrast, functional sensitivity, as measured by the input-output Jacobian, reliably tracks this capability. We further provide an analytic account showing that this disparity arises from objective design, as existing losses explicitly constrain embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping unconstrained. These results suggest that global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence and establish functional sensitivity as a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.

papers.title: Revealing Token-Level Importance in Conditional Molecular Design Through Kullback–Leibler Divergence
papers.research_question: How can we explain conditional molecular design models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process to reveal token-level importance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to interpret conditional molecular design models using Kullback-Leibler Divergence to quantify the token-level importance of property conditions during generation.
papers.conclusion: Introduced a novel method for interpreting conditional molecular design models using KL divergence to quantify the influence of property conditions.
future_direction: Analyze how perturbations on the most important tokens affect predicted property values
Compare the explainability method with other approaches in the literature
Assess generalization to other textual- and graph-based molecular representations
papers.abstract: Conditional molecular design using transformer-based models can accelerate drug discovery, but their black-box nature limits interpretability. We propose a method to explain these models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process. Our approach uses the Kullback–Leibler Divergence to measure the difference between conditional and unconditional output distributions at each generation step. This allows us to identify the token-level importance of a sequence for specific desired conditions.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models.
